title: Thor in the Land of the Giants

blocks.text: Once, Thor set out on a journey in his chariot, pulled by two goats, and Loki went with him. That night they stopped at a farmer's cottage. Thor killed his two goats, cooked them in a pot and invited the farmer's family to share the supper. "But put all the bones on the goatskins," he said. "Don't break any."
The farmer's son, Thialfi, did not listen. He split one of the leg bones open with his knife to get at the tasty marrow inside.
In the morning, Thor raised his hammer over the goatskins and blessed them. At once the goats jumped up, alive again! But one of them was limping on a lame back leg.

Thor's face grew dark. He gripped his hammer so hard that his knuckles turned white. The farmer and his family were terrified and begged for mercy. "Take anything we have!" they cried. When Thor saw how frightened they were, his anger melted away. He took the farmer's son, Thialfi, and his daughter, Roskva, to be his servants. They went with him ever after, and Thialfi was the fastest runner of all.

Thor left his goats with the farmer and set off on foot toward Giantland with Loki, Thialfi and Roskva. They crossed a deep sea and walked into a great forest. When night came, they found a strange house with a wide doorway as big as the whole house, and a smaller room off to one side. They lay down to sleep.

At midnight there was a terrible earthquake. The ground rumbled and shook. Thor's friends hid in the little side room, and Thor sat in the doorway with his hammer, ready to fight. All night long they heard a great roaring and rumbling.

At dawn Thor went outside. There, lying in the forest, was an enormous giant, fast asleep and snoring. That was the rumbling they had heard! The giant woke up and stood up, so tall that even Thor did not dare to swing at him.

"My name is Skrymir," said the giant. "And I know you, you're Thor. But what have you done with my glove?" He bent down and picked it up. The house they had slept in was his glove! The little side room was its thumb!

Skrymir offered to travel with them, and to carry all their food in his bag. That evening he lay down under an oak tree and fell asleep. Thor tried to open the bag to get their supper, but he could not untie a single knot. He was so angry that he took his hammer and hit Skrymir on the head.
Skrymir woke up. "Did a leaf fall on my head?" he asked. "Have you had your supper, Thor?" And he went back to sleep.

At midnight, Thor hit him again, even harder. "Was that an acorn?" asked Skrymir sleepily. Just before dawn, Thor hit him a third time, as hard as he possibly could. Skrymir sat up and rubbed his cheek. "There must be birds up in this tree," he said. "I think some moss fell on my face." Then he got up. "You're nearly at the city of Utgard," he said. "But be careful. You think I'm big. Wait until you see the giants there!" And off he went into the forest.

At noon, they saw a city on a plain. It was so tall that they had to bend their heads right back to see the top. The gate was locked, but they squeezed in between the bars. Inside was a huge hall, full of giants sitting on benches, and there sat the king, Utgard-Loki.
"So this little fellow must be Thor," said the king. "Well, nobody can stay here unless they're the best at something. What can you do?"
"I can eat faster than anyone," said Loki.

So Utgard-Loki called a giant named Logi. They put a long trough full of meat on the floor, with Loki at one end and Logi at the other, and they started eating. They met exactly in the middle. But Loki had eaten only the meat. Logi had eaten the meat, and the bones, and the wooden trough too! So Loki lost.
"What can the young man do?" asked the king.
"I can run," said Thialfi.
So Utgard-Loki called a young giant named Hugi to race him. Three times they raced, and each time Hugi won easily. The third time, he finished before Thialfi was halfway there.
"And what can you do, Thor?" asked the king.
"I can drink more than anyone," said Thor.
So the king's servant brought in a long drinking horn. "A good drinker can empty this in one drink," said Utgard-Loki. "Most people need two. Even a weakling can do it in three."

Thor was thirsty. He took a huge, long drink. But when he looked in, the horn was hardly any emptier. He took a second drink, even longer. It went down only a little. He took a third drink with all his might, and the horn was still nearly full. He gave it back, red in the face.
"Let's try something easy," said the king. "Our children like to lift my cat off the floor."

A big grey cat came into the hall. Thor put his hand under its belly and lifted. But the cat just arched its back higher and higher, and no matter how hard Thor pulled, he could only lift one of its paws off the floor.
"Let someone wrestle me, then!" roared Thor.

"Nobody here would bother," said the king. "But you may wrestle my old nurse, Elli." And in came a toothless old woman. The harder Thor pushed, the firmer she stood. Then she began to push back, and at last Thor fell down onto one knee.
Thor and his friends were very ashamed. But the king gave them a good dinner and a bed for the night. In the morning, he walked them out of the city. And then he told them the truth.
"Now that you're outside my city," he said, "I can tell you. If I had known how strong you were, I would never have let you in. I have been tricking you all along with magic.

"I was Skrymir, the giant in the forest. I tied up the bag with magic iron wire, so you couldn't open it. And when you hit me with your hammer, I put a mountain in the way. Look over there, and you will see three deep valleys in that mountain, made by your three blows!
"Logi, who ate the trough, was really wildfire, which burns up everything. Hugi, who raced Thialfi, was really my thought, and nothing is faster than thought.
"The end of the drinking horn was dipped in the sea. You drank so much that the sea went down! Look at the shore, and you'll see it. That's why the sea goes out at low tide.

"The cat was really the Midgard Serpent, the great snake that lies around the whole world. When you lifted one paw, we were all terrified! And my old nurse Elli was Old Age. No one has ever beaten Old Age, and nobody ever will. Yet you only fell to one knee.
"Now go home, and don't come back!"

Thor raised his hammer in anger. But when he turned to strike, Utgard-Loki was gone. And when he turned back toward the city, the whole city had disappeared, and there was nothing there but a wide, empty plain.

A simplified retelling of “Thor's Journey to the Land of the Giants” in The Prose Edda, translated by I. A. Blackwell (1847). The original is listed under Other versions. Blackwell spells Thialfi “Thjalfi” and his sister Roskva “Roska.”
